titulo: Norway Nears Goal to Sell only Electric New Cars

fuente.licencia: Dominio público (VOA, gobierno de EE. UU.)
fuente.nota: Texto recortado por párrafos; sin cambios en las frases.

parrafos: The Norwegian Road Federation (OFV), an automotive industry group, estimates that nearly 96 percent of new cars registered in Norway in January were all-electric. No other country has such a high rate of electric car (EV) ownership.

The OFV noted that of the 9,343 new cars sold last month in Norway, 8,954 of them were all-electric. Of the 50 most-sold models, only two were non-electric. The first of those came in 33rd place among the 50 models, the federation said.
The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) reported the share of electric cars in Europe was just 13.6 percent during 2024. That was the first recorded decrease since 2020.

OFV director Oyvind Solberg Thorsen said in a statement, "We've never seen this before...If the rest of the year continues like this, we will very soon be close to the 2025 goal." He noted that reaching 100 percent of the goal means to continue to offer the “incentives that make it profitable to choose an electric car over other models.”

Even though it is a major oil and gas producer, Norway aims to only sell "zero emission" new vehicles starting in 2025. That goal is 10 years ahead of the target set by the European Union (EU). Norway is not a member of the EU.

One difference between the EU and Norway’s method is that Norway has not banned the sale of cars with engines that burn fuel. Instead, Norway offers a number of tax breaks to EV manufacturers and owners. On the other hand, the country heavily taxes gas-powered vehicles.

For example, Norwegian EV owners do not have to pay road tolls and receive free parking in public car parks. EVs are also permitted to use parts of roads normally saved for public transportation vehicles.

Frode Hvattum is a 50-year-old father of three who owns two EVs. He told the French News Agency AFP he started buying EVs because of his concern for the environment and for the benefits of driving them.
He lives in an area near Oslo where the streets are full of Teslas, Audis and Volkswagens. Some less costly Chinese EVs are increasingly appearing too.
Many homes have a device to charge, or supply electricity to, their EV’s battery. Norway also has a large national network of superfast charging stations.

Having a nationwide charging network was important for Hvattum, who, like many Norwegians, often travels by car to his second home in the mountains several hours outside Oslo. He said he finds it easy to plan and make trips with numerous charging stations available.
"You don't have to plan your trip as much as before," Hvattum said. He added that he uses the 15-to-20-minute charging breaks his vehicle needs to make it up to the mountains to shop for food.
Even if EV sales fail to meet the 100 percent mark this year, experts say Norway can still be seen as having met its goal.
titulo_es: Noruega, cerca de su objetivo de vender solo coches nuevos eléctricos
resumen_es: Casi el 96 % de los coches nuevos matriculados en Noruega en enero eran eléctricos gracias a incentivos fiscales y a una amplia red de recarga, muy por delante del resto de Europa.

ideas_clave.idea: In January almost 96 percent of the new cars registered in Norway were fully electric, an unmatched rate worldwide.
By contrast, electric cars accounted for under 14 percent of sales across Europe in 2024, their first decline since 2020.
The industry group believes the 2025 target is within reach, provided that the incentives making electric cars profitable remain in place.
Despite being a large oil and gas producer, Norway aims for zero-emission new car sales from 2025, a decade earlier than the EU.
Rather than banning combustion engines, Norway relies on tax advantages and perks for electric car owners and heavy taxes on petrol cars.
A driver near Oslo explains that he chose electric cars for environmental reasons and practical benefits; cheaper Chinese models are also becoming common.
Home chargers and a dense national network of fast-charging stations make long trips easy to plan.
Experts consider that Norway will have achieved its aim even if sales fall slightly short of 100 percent.

resumen_modelo: The text reports that Norway is very close to its goal of selling only electric new cars. According to the national road federation, nearly 96 percent of the new vehicles registered in January were fully electric, a share unmatched anywhere else, whereas in Europe as a whole electric cars represented just 13.6 percent of sales in 2024, their first fall since 2020. Paradoxically, although Norway is a major oil and gas producer, it intends to sell only zero-emission new cars from 2025, ten years ahead of the European Union. Instead of banning combustion engines, the country has chosen to reward electric car buyers with tax breaks, exemptions from road tolls, free public parking and access to bus lanes, while heavily taxing petrol vehicles. The industry warns that these incentives must be maintained to reach the target. The experience of a driver near Oslo illustrates the importance of infrastructure: thanks to home chargers and a nationwide network of fast-charging stations, journeys to the mountains are easy to plan. Finally, experts believe that the goal can be considered met even if sales do not quite reach 100 percent.
